A well-calibrated thinker who says 'I'm 70% sure' is correct approximately 70% of the time on claims of that type.
models.origin: Philip Tetlock (Expert Political Judgment, 2005; Superforecasting, 2015); decision science and forecasting literature; meteorology as a model domain.
models.when_to_use: When making predictions; when communicating about uncertain outcomes; when evaluating the track record of an expert or forecaster; when making decisions that depend on probability estimates; when designing processes that aggregate multiple uncertain judgments.
how_to_apply: Track your predictions and their outcomes over time.
For each domain where you make predictions, assess whether your '70% confident' claims come true approximately 70% of the time.
Identify systematic patterns: are you overconfident in some domains and underconfident in others?
Correct for known biases: if you are systematically overconfident about X, adjust your expressed confidence downward in that domain.
Use reference class forecasting: before estimating the probability for your specific case, ask 'what is the base rate for this type of event?'
Update calibration as new evidence accumulates.
models.dewey_connection: Calibrated uncertainty is the quantitative form of Dewey's intellectual virtues of Suspended Judgment and Intellectual Responsibility. Dewey insists that the responsible thinker proportions belief to evidence; calibration is the empirical measure of whether a thinker actually does this. Tetlock's research on superforecasters shows that calibration is a trainable skill — directly consistent with Dewey's view that intellectual virtues are developed, not innate.
models.example: A superforecaster who said '75% confident' on 100 different predictions reviews their track record: of those 100 claims, approximately 73 turned out to be true. This is well-calibrated. A poorly calibrated forecaster who said '95% confident' on the same set of predictions had only 65 come true — systematically overconfident.
models.common_misuse: Treating calibration as the only epistemic virtue — valuing accurate uncertainty assessment so highly that decisive action becomes impossible. Calibrated uncertainty is valuable for improving decision quality; it is not an end in itself. A well-calibrated forecast of '55% probable' should still lead to action when the expected value of acting is positive.

models.name: Epistemic Humility
models.definition: The recognition that one's knowledge is limited, fallible, and shaped by one's perspective and experience — and the corresponding openness to revision in light of new evidence or argument. Epistemic humility is not skepticism (doubt about whether anything can be known) but calibration (confidence proportioned to evidence and acknowledgment of limits).
models.origin: Philosophical tradition from Socrates ('I know that I know nothing') through modern epistemology; central to scientific method; developed in practical terms by Philip Tetlock's work on forecasting.
models.when_to_use: As a constant background disposition in all reasoning — particularly active when reasoning in domains where you have strong prior commitments, limited experience, or a track record of overconfidence; when presenting findings to others; when making decisions with significant irreversibility.
how_to_apply: Regularly ask: what would change my mind about this?
Distinguish between what you know from direct experience, what you know from reliable evidence, what you believe based on inference, and what you assume without examination.
Take seriously the possibility that you are wrong about things you feel most confident about — historical track records of confident experts being systematically wrong are extensive.
When presenting conclusions, explicitly acknowledge what you do not know and what could change your assessment.
Resist the pressure to project more confidence than you have — epistemic cowardice masquerading as clarity harms those who depend on your judgment.
models.dewey_connection: Epistemic humility is the dispositional foundation of Dewey's entire account of reflective thinking. Every phase of Dewey's inquiry arc — from willingness to sustain perplexity (Phase 1), to holding hypotheses tentatively (Phase 3), to genuinely submitting them to test (Phase 5) — requires epistemic humility as its motivating virtue. Without it, the inquiry collapses at each phase into premature closure. Paul-Elder's Intellectual Humility is the named trait; this model provides the epistemological grounding for why it matters.
models.example: A senior researcher who has spent 20 years studying a topic encounters a replication study that challenges findings they helped establish. Epistemic humility: 'This is a serious challenge to conclusions I have been confident about. I need to understand the methodology of the replication study, assess whether the discrepancy reveals a flaw in my original work or a limitation of the replication, and update my published conclusions accordingly if the evidence warrants.' This is the disposition Dewey describes as essential to genuine inquiry.
models.common_misuse: Treating epistemic humility as a requirement to express equal uncertainty about all claims — as if saying 'I could be wrong' must accompany every assertion regardless of evidential strength. Epistemic humility is about accurate calibration, not uniform hedging. It is equally epistemically irresponsible to express false uncertainty about well-established facts as it is to express false certainty about speculative ones.
